content_metadata.description: An informative and engaging video that explains the concept of monoclonal antibodies, their production process, applications, and limitations.

qAndA.answer: The mouse's spleen is where B cells are concentrated. It is removed and the B cells are isolated to be used in the production process.
qAndA.question: What is the role of the spleen in the production of monoclonal antibodies?

qAndA.answer: B cells don't naturally divide, but tumor cells do. Fusing them allows the combined cell to both produce antibodies and multiply rapidly.
qAndA.question: Why are tumor cells fused with B cells to create Hybridoma cells?

qAndA.answer: In pregnancy tests, monoclonal antibodies bind specifically to the HCG hormone found in the urine of pregnant women, leading to a color change on the test strip.
qAndA.question: What is an example of how monoclonal antibodies are used in diagnostic testing?

qAndA.answer: They are expensive and time-consuming to produce. They also can have more side effects than initially expected.
qAndA.question: What are two limitations of monoclonal antibodies?

qAndA.answer: Monoclonal antibodies have the potential to be highly specific and effective in targeting diseases. Scientists are actively working to improve their production and reduce side effects.
qAndA.question: Why are scientists still optimistic about the future of monoclonal antibodies despite their limitations?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Antibodies are the warriors inside our body. They are part of our immune system, recognizing
and fighting against bad foreign invaders called antigens. Antibodies combine to a broad
range of antigens and are produced by cells of the immune system, known as B cells. To
learn more about antibodies and antigens, watch this video. Antibodies can be used for medical
and diagnostic applications in the form of monoclonal antibodies. So what are monoclonal
antibodies? The word monoclonal means a single clone. Monoclonal antibodies are identical
antibodies, produced in laboratories from a single clone of immune cells. The cloned
immune cells are genetically completely identical, and so the antibodies they produce are also
identical to one another, which is perfect. To work properly, we need large numbers of
identical antibodies. Monoclonal antibodies have a high specificity, which means they can
recognize and bind to a single antigen binding site. This means they are targeted to a specific
antigen and is a key trait that makes them useful in diagnosing and treating diseases.
So how they produce? Well, first off, we need an immune system, which is why we use mice.
In a laboratory, a mouse is vaccinated with the target antigen. This stimulates the B cells
found in the spleen to produce antibodies against the target antigen. The spleen of the
mouse is then removed. The B cells in the spleen are isolated and fused with a tumor cell.
We need to fuse the antibody producing B cells with a tumor cell because the B cells don't
have the ability to divide, but tumors, however, do divide easily. This fusion cell is called
a hybridoma cell. The hybridoma cells reproduce rapidly to make cloned cells, which all make
the same antibody. These monoclonal antibodies are collected and purified, ready for use.
They match up perfectly with the target antigens in the body and are made in huge quantities.
Monoclonal antibodies are potentially really exciting and can be used in a number of ways.
I bet you didn't know antibodies were used in pregnancy tests. Monoclonal antibodies
on the pregnancy test stick bind to the HCG hormone found in the urine of pregnant women,
causing a color change. Monoclonal antibodies can target the antigens on cancer cells and
be used in a number of ways. Firstly, I combine them with an anti-cancer drug which can then
accurately locate and target only the cancer cells or avoiding the healthy cells. Secondly,
for detection, they can carry special markers which show doctors where the cancerous cells are
starting to build up. Thirdly, they can be used to trigger the body's own immune system to
recognise and kill the cancer cells. They can also be used to identify other diseases and locate
blood clots. So those are a few uses, but are they all good? We've seen the positives.
So what are some criticisms? They are expensive and time consuming to produce. They have more side
effects than expected and they are too specific, meaning that whilst yes, they can diagnose and
attack diseases, they only can attack one type each time. A more diverse and adaptable solution
would be better. The potential power of monoclonal antibodies is clear, they are not yet as widely used
as everyone hoped when they were first developed, but scientists are working hard to make them better
and safer for wider use. Their journey is just beginning. If you liked the video, give it a thumbs
up and don't forget to subscribe, comment below if you have any questions. Why not check out
our few scrap as well? Until next time!

youtube_description:
The soldiers of our body are the antibodies. They work with our immune system to identify and combat undesirable foreign invaders known as antigens.

B-cells, immune system cells that create antibodies, may attach to a wide variety of antigens.
Watch this video to learn more about antibodies and antigens.

Monoclonal antibodies, which are variations of antibodies, can be employed for therapeutic and diagnostic purposes.

What exactly are monoclonal antibodies then?
